newsitem.title: USA: No huge growth for aluminum auto body sheet - CRU.
newsitem.headline: No huge growth for aluminum auto body sheet - CRU.

text.p: Aluminum is unlikely to see huge demand for auto body uses, and may well lose some of its gains to plastic in the future, analyst Kelly Driscoll of CRU International said.
Driscoll, speaking at Gorham/Intertech Consulting's "The Aluminum Scrap Gap" conference, said there was hope in the aluminum industry that auto body applications may be the next can stock market.
Aluminum can stock for beverage cans is a huge consumer of the metal.
But Driscoll warned that demand for aluminum in car structures will "fall well short of the dizzy heights of the can stock market".
Current use of aluminum in car structures and exterior panels is still limited to 45,000 to 50,000 tonnes a year, compared to 40 million tonnes for steel.

"What should be borne in mind also is that aluminium is not just in competition with steel, but that plastics offer many advantages also as a material for hang-on parts, whilst offering possible long-term solutions to the problem of how to increase car production flexibility," Driscoll said.
For the next five to ten years, growth in aluminum auto structures will be incremental, largely in exterior panels especially in North America.
"However, the growth in the market will most likely mean that aluminium auto body sheet consumption reaches over 100,000 tonnes per year soon into the next century," Driscoll said.
A key driver of the growth in aluminum structured vehicles is also the expected rise of the electric car market which will largely favor aluminum designs, Driscoll said.
Aluminium body sheet consumption is forecast to reach 500,000 to 700,000 tonnes in 20 years, according to CRU.
"If the aluminium mass volume design is not introduced in North America, then the market for auto body sheet will be almost half that forecast," Driscoll said.
Much will also depend on how many electric vehicles will be produced with aluminium benefiting more if environmental regulations become much tighter.
